strengths: Novel and well-motivated research question: the paper appears to be the first to investigate brain predictive coding from the decoding (fMRI-to-text) perspective rather than the encoding perspective, providing a genuinely new angle bridging cognitive neuroscience theory and NLP decoding.

The preliminary verification experiment (Section 2) is a sensible and transparent analysis, replicating the Caucheteux et al. (2023) encoding result to justify the ROI selection and the prediction-distance design choices before committing to the architecture.

The paper adopts the leakage-free cross-subject splitting protocol of Yin et al. (2023), explicitly acknowledging known data-contamination problems in prior fMRI-to-text work — a commendable methodological decision.

The evaluation goes beyond headline metrics: ROI-selection analysis (None/Random/Whole/BPC) serves as a control against the concern that any side network helps, the prediction-distance analysis ties decoding behavior back to the verification experiment, and the appendix error-distribution analysis with the 'information loss slope' is a creative diagnostic that supports the claimed mechanism (predictive coding mitigating information loss at frame ends).

Hyperparameters, dataset preprocessing, splitting, and training details are documented in the appendix, and limitations are candidly acknowledged (single dataset, cross-subject-only splitting, fixed window l=2).
weaknesses: Evidence for the state-of-the-art claim is thin: only one baseline (UniCoRN) is compared. Tang et al. (2023) and BrainLLM are excluded due to 'incompatible settings,' which substantially weakens the SOTA claim; compatibility adaptation or an approximated reimplementation would have been more convincing.

No statistical significance testing or multi-seed variance is reported for the main results. Several reported differences are small or mixed (e.g., UniCoRN wins ROUGE-1 R in some settings; PREDFT's ROUGE-1 F advantage at length 10 is marginal), so it is hard to judge robustness of the improvements.

Absolute decoding quality is very low (BLEU-1 27.8%, BLEU-4 0.54), and the case-study claims are overstated relative to the shown outputs: e.g., interpreting 'his girl sleep' as decoding 'he and Mary prepare to sleep,' or 'good dream' as conveying 'the best dream,' stretches the evidence; decoded text remains largely incoherent.

There is a residual confound the ablations do not fully rule out: the side network is trained to predict future ground-truth words, and decoder tokens may attend to predictive representations after the current time step. The Random-ROI control helps, but the paper does not analyze whether gains stem from genuine brain-signal-derived prediction versus the side network acting as a learned language prior, and the choice of cross-attention mask allowing 'future' access deserves more scrutiny.

Hyper-parameter λ appears selected per sequence length (1 for length 10, 0.5 otherwise) with no stated validation set or selection protocol, raising the possibility of test-set tuning; similarly, prediction distance d is analyzed post hoc.

Evaluation relies solely on n-gram overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE), which are weak proxies for semantic reconstruction quality in open-vocabulary generation; no human or semantic-similarity (e.g., embedding-based) evaluation is provided.

Generalizability is limited: a single dataset (Narratives), cross-subject splitting only, and fixed l=2 due to compute constraints — all acknowledged, but they restrict the strength of the central claims at this stage.

Presentation has clarity issues: several notational/typographical errors (e.g., 'The cross attention if formularized,' inconsistent dimension notation in Equation 1, 'PREDFT' vs 'PredFT'), and the methodology section leans on reproduced Transformer equations that add length without insight.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and relatively unexplored question: whether brain predictive coding, previously studied only from the encoding side, can be exploited for fMRI-to-text decoding. The framing connecting predictive coding theory to language reconstruction is novel.

The preliminary verification experiment (Section 2) replicates and extends encoding-side findings (Caucheteux et al.) and is used to motivate concrete design choices (six ROIs, prediction distance d), giving the method a neuroscientifically grounded motivation rather than a purely architectural one.

The experimental analysis is broad: ROI-selection comparisons (None/Random/Whole/BPC), prediction-distance sweeps, positional decoding-error analysis with a proposed 'information loss slope' metric, ablations, and hyper-parameter sensitivity are all included, and the analysis of information loss due to fMRI's low temporal resolution is a genuinely useful observation for the field.

The authors adopt the leakage-free cross-subject splitting protocol of Yin et al. [43], addressing a known data-leakage problem in prior work (UniCoRN), and are transparent about limitations (single dataset, no per-subject experiments, fixed window length).
weaknesses: The main comparison rests on a single baseline (UniCoRN). Exclusion of Tang et al. [33] and BrainLLM [42] is justified only vaguely ('model settings aren't compatible'), leaving the SOTA claim weakly supported. Moreover, PREDFT w/o SideNet underperforms UniCoRN in most settings, and the authors attribute this to UniCoRN's pretrained language model — this makes it unclear whether the side-network gains reflect predictive coding or simply added model capacity relative to a from-scratch baseline.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals on the decoding results, or multiple-seed variance reporting is provided. Several reported differences (e.g., ROUGE-1 F between models in Table 1) are small, and with test-set-based tuning of lambda (best value differs per sequence length) and ROI configurations, there is a risk of selection effects; a validation protocol is not clearly described.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code or configuration release is mentioned, key architectural details (e.g., exact 3D-CNN structure, dm, k*, how ROI one-dimensional vectors are formed from the Destrieux atlas) are underspecified, and the splitting implementation of [43] is not described in enough detail to reimplement.

Evaluation relies exclusively on n-gram overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE). The case study in Table 3 shows that both models' outputs are largely ungrammatical and semantically loose; 'more real than any dream' vs. 'a more than normal just good dream' suggests the headline BLEU-1 improvement may overstate genuine decoding quality. No semantic similarity or human evaluation is attempted.

The causal link between the predictive-coding verification experiment and the decoding gains is asserted rather than demonstrated: the consistency of the d=4 peak across encoding and decoding is correlational, and alternative explanations (e.g., extra temporal context, more parameters in the cross-attention pathway) are not ruled out by the 'Whole' ROI ablation, which also performs reasonably well.

The paper contains presentation defects that reduce clarity: notation inconsistencies in Equation 1 (dimension mismatch between R^{k×dm} and the stated output shape), grammatical errors ('The cross attention if formularized'), and figures whose details are hard to verify from the text.

strengths: Novel and interesting research question: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to explicitly connect brain predictive coding theory to the fMRI-to-text decoding perspective, rather than only the encoding perspective, which is a genuinely fresh angle for the decoding literature.

The design is grounded in a preliminary verification experiment (Section 2) that measures prediction scores between LM activations and brain responses, and the identified prediction distance (~d=4) is later shown to align with the decoding-optimal prediction distance (Figure 4), which is a coherent empirical story.

The experimental design addresses a known reproducibility/validity problem in this area: the authors adopt the cross-subject splitting protocol of Yin et al. [43] to avoid the data leakage identified in UniCoRN's setup, which is a methodologically responsible choice.

The analysis is more thorough than typical: ROI selection ablations (None/Random/Whole/BPC), prediction distance analysis, hyper-parameter sensitivity for λ, and a creative decoding error-position analysis with an 'information loss slope' index that gives mechanistic insight into why late words in a TR are hard to decode.

The paper is candid about limitations (single dataset, cross-subject split only, fixed window length l=2), and the discussion fairly presents the controversy around why LMs fit brain data (Antonello & Huth).
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is thin: only UniCoRN is compared, and the strongest related systems (Tang et al. [33], BrainLLM [42]) are excluded on compatibility grounds. The state-of-the-art claim therefore rests on a single comparison under a changed data-splitting protocol, which weakens the headline claim.

The causal attribution to 'predictive coding' is confounded. The six BPC ROIs (superior temporal sulcus, angular/supramarginal gyri, inferior frontal gyrus) are also the classic language-processing regions, so they may simply be the most information-rich voxels for decoding rather than specifically predictive ones. The fact that 'Whole' cortex performs nearly as well while 'Random' fails suggests the benefit may come from informative language regions generally, not prediction per se; the paper's conclusion that 'predictive coding information only contains in specific regions' does not rule this out. A control with non-predictive but language-involved ROIs, or a side network trained on past rather than future words, would be needed.

No statistical significance testing or multi-run variance is reported. Several improvements are small (e.g., BLEU-2/3/4 differences of a few tenths of a percent, ROUGE-1 recall often favoring UniCoRN), and given the noise level implied by the verification experiment's confidence intervals, the reliability of the gains is unclear.

No pretrained language model is used in PREDFT while the baseline uses BART, confounding the architectural comparison; the ablation result that PREDFT w/o SideNet underperforms UniCoRN is attributed to the pretrained LM, but this is not directly tested (e.g., by initializing the decoder from BART).

The actual decoding quality, as shown in the case study, remains largely incoherent; the SOTA claim is driven by low-level n-gram metrics, and no semantic/embedding-based metrics (e.g., BERTScore, perplexity-based measures) or human evaluation are used, even though the paper's motivation centers on semantic content.

Reproducibility is limited: no mention of released code or preprocessing scripts, and key details (e.g., exact preprocessing pipeline, dataset split files, number of runs) are only partially specified; results appear to be from single runs.
Only one dataset (Narratives) is used, and the λ hyper-parameter must be re-tuned per sequence length, which raises mild concerns about robustness and generalization of the approach.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence, e.g., 'first to try decoding one-minute of fMRI data' is a marginal contribution, and the writing contains minor grammatical issues (e.g., 'The cross attention if formularized').

strengths: The paper connects an interesting neuroscience theory (predictive coding) to fMRI-to-text decoding, providing a motivated and reasonably well-executed exploration of a timely problem at the NLP/neuroscience interface.

A preliminary verification experiment (Section 2, Figure 9, Figure 12) replicates the Caucheteux et al. (2023) style brain-score analysis and identifies prediction-related ROIs before building the model, giving the design some empirical grounding rather than being purely architecture-driven.

Experiments cover two standard naturalistic comprehension datasets (LeBel, Narratives), both within-subject and cross-subject settings, and multiple recent baselines (Tang et al., BrainLLM, MapGuide, UniCoRN), including evaluation under the leakage-free splitting protocol of Yin et al. (2023).

The paper is unusually thorough in analysis: ROI selection ablations (Random/Whole/BPC), prediction length/distance sweeps, loss-weight (lambda) sensitivity, a chance-level (shuffled-fMRI) control, an information-loss error-position analysis, and qualitative case studies with honestly negative observations (all models produce mostly incoherent text).

Reproducibility support is comparatively good: datasets are public, preprocessing, parcellations, hyper-parameters, tokenizer choices, and hardware are specified, and appendix materials (notation table, framework figures, per-subject results) are provided.
weaknesses: The central causal claim — that *predictive coding* specifically improves decoding — is only weakly supported. The side network is essentially an auxiliary sequence predictor over selected voxels; the observed gains from BPC ROIs could reflect general informativeness of language-processing cortex (BPC includes auditory cortex, PFC, Broca) rather than predictive function per se. A control with non-predictive but language-relevant ROIs is missing.

Absolute decoding quality is very low (BLEU-2/3/4 near zero, BERTScore gaps small, case studies largely incoherent), so gains of a few BLEU-1 points on three subjects are fragile evidence. No statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple-run variance are reported for the main decoding results, and only 3 subjects are used for the key within-subject claims.

Potential test-set selection concern: the prediction length l and distance d appear to be tuned per setting (e.g., best performance at d≈4), and the main-table configuration relative to these sweeps is not clearly stated. Selecting (l, d) based on test-set performance could inflate reported results; a validation-based selection protocol should be made explicit.

There is a circularity risk in the pipeline: ROIs for the side network are 'verified' on the same datasets (and same subjects) later used for decoding evaluation, so the verification experiment does not serve as independent evidence.

The architecture itself is fairly standard (CNN/linear encoders + Transformer encoders/decoders + cross-attention fusion); the novelty is mainly in the motivation and the side-network training objective, and the 'predictive coding attention' is ordinary cross-attention with a mask — the connection to predictive coding theory is more framing than mechanism.

Baseline comparability is imperfect: baselines are reimplemented 'following the proposed papers' under the authors' splits and settings, and PREDFT w/o SideNet sometimes underperforms UniCoRN, complicating attribution of improvements to the proposed idea versus implementation details. BERTScore results are mixed relative to the best baseline.

Some writing/clarity issues: figure caption errors (Figure 9 'sub-figure (a) to (c)' should read (d) to (f)), apparent labeling inconsistency in Figure 2 (M_θDec in side network), and occasional unclear statements (e.g., 'the side network brings more advancement' phrasing).

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and timely question: whether predictive coding, as an account of brain-language alignment (Caucheteux et al. 2023), can be exploited for fMRI-to-text decoding, going beyond purely architectural work in this area.

The experimental scope is reasonably broad: two datasets (LeBel, Narratives), within-subject and cross-subject settings, multiple fMRI window lengths, ROI-selection analyses, hyper-parameter sweeps, ablations, a chance-level control (shuffled fMRI inputs), and a decoding-error positional analysis proposing an 'information loss slope' metric.

The authors are aware of data-contamination issues in prior cross-subject evaluation (Xi et al. 2023) and adopt the leakage-aware split of Yin et al. (2023), which is a methodologically responsible choice.

The verification experiment (Section 2) is a sensible preliminary check, and the ROI-selection results (BPC > Whole > Random) are consistent with the verification analysis, giving internal coherence to the story.
The limitations, ethics statement, and discussion candidly acknowledge key weaknesses, including that current fMRI temporal resolution may make word-level decoding fundamentally hard.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'excellent decoding performance' is not supported by the actual evidence. The decoded text (Table 8) is largely incoherent; BLEU-4 is below 2% for all models; BERTScore gaps between PREDFT and baselines are small (~1 point). The absolute decoding quality is far too poor to support strong claims of superiority, and the case study shows outputs like 'It's a more than normal just good dream about to said.'

Evaluation validity is questionable: BLEU-1/ROUGE-1 on near-random open-vocabulary generation can be substantially driven by unigram frequency priors rather than genuine neural decoding. The paper provides no significance testing, no variance over multiple runs, and no human or semantic-level evaluation, despite acknowledging in the Discussion that word-level metrics are inadequate for this task.

Reported results contain anomalies that are not explained: e.g., PREDFT w/o SideNet in Table 1 has ROUGE1-P of 49-55 with ROUGE1-R of ~15-18, suggesting very short generated outputs, yet BLEU-1 remains comparable to baselines; Sub-2 'None' ROUGE1-R of 50.28 deviates wildly from all other entries. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the quantitative results.

No statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported for the main decoding comparisons, and only 3 subjects are evaluated on LeBel's dataset, so the claimed improvements over baselines (e.g., BLEU-1 gains of 1-7 points) may not be robust.

The novelty of the verification experiment is limited: it closely replicates the analysis design of Caucheteux et al. (2023) (brain scores, prediction scores, prediction length/distance) on the same datasets, so the theoretical contribution is largely confirmatory rather than new.

There is a causal ambiguity the paper does not resolve: the side network is trained with ground-truth future words as decoder input, and its representations are fused via cross-attention. The paper does not demonstrate that the side-network representation actually encodes future content recovered from brain signals (e.g., via probing or ablation of the prediction training objective) versus acting as a generic regularizer or extra capacity; the strong w/o-SideNet degradation could stem from architectural capacity or optimization effects rather than 'brain prediction'.

The gap between the verification analysis and the decoding model is thin: the mask design (Fig. 4) allows tokens to attend to 'future' ROI representations after time t, but the actual content of these representations is never analyzed, leaving the mechanistic claim about predictive coding speculative.

Reproducibility is not adequately supported: no mention of released code, and many details (3D-CNN architecture specifics, training data amounts, decoding hyper-parameters at inference) are dispersed or missing; given 200M parameters trained from scratch, independent reproduction would be difficult.

Writing quality is uneven (e.g., grammatical errors in the baseline descriptions, 'capture the simulate the brain responses'), and Figure 12's Narratives verification result is relegated to an appendix with only a single setting (l=2), weakening the generality of the verification claims across datasets.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to systematically connect predictive coding theory to fMRI-to-text decoding, moving beyond purely architectural work (Tang et al., UniCoRN, BrainLLM, MapGuide) toward a neuroscientifically grounded design.

The preliminary verification experiment (Section 2) is a sensible design that establishes the empirical motivation before proposing the model: prediction scores over prediction length/distance, plus ROI-level analysis, replicate and extend Caucheteux et al. (2023) in a decoding-relevant way, and the decoder results in Section 4.4 mirror the verification results, giving the paper internal coherence.

PREDFT is clearly specified: the main/side network decomposition, the predictive-coding attention with its custom mask (Figure 4), FIR-based BOLD latency compensation, and the shared-embedding joint training objective are all described in enough detail to reimplement, with hyper-parameters in Appendix A.

The experiments address the field's known pitfalls: the authors explicitly adopt the leakage-safe splitting protocol of Yin et al. (2023) for cross-subject decoding on Narratives, run a chance-level (shuffled-fMRI) control, an ablation without the side network, a hyper-parameter (λ) sweep, and per-subject robustness checks in the appendix.

The information-loss analysis (Appendix D, information loss slope φ) is an interesting empirical observation about fMRI temporal resolution and late-word decoding errors, and shows the side network partially mitigates it—this adds value beyond leaderboard claims.

Experiments cover both within-subject (LeBel) and cross-subject (Narratives) settings with multiple sequence lengths and reasonable baseline coverage, and the writing is generally clear with honest acknowledgment of limitations (low absolute quality, word-level vs. semantic evaluation).
weaknesses: No statistical significance testing or variance reporting for the main decoding results: only 3 subjects are used for the headline within-subject comparisons, and improvements of a few BLEU/ROUGE points (e.g., BERTScore gaps of <1 vs. BrainLLM) are asserted as 'outperforming' without confidence intervals or tests, weakening the central empirical claim.

Attribution of gains to predictive coding is not fully isolated: PREDFT differs from baselines in many ways (end-to-end training, architecture, tokenizer, training-from-scratch), and PREDFT w/o SideNet is the only controlled comparison; the side network adds parameters and an auxiliary LM loss, so gains could partly reflect capacity/regularization rather than brain prediction specifically. An auxiliary-loss control on non-predictive ROIs of matched size would strengthen the claim (the 'Random' ROI condition partially covers this, but the results are noisy).

Absolute decoding quality remains very low (BLEU-4 mostly <2, case studies show largely disfluent output), so the practical significance of the improvements is modest; the paper itself concedes word-level metrics may be inappropriate but does not adopt any semantic-level or human evaluation.

The prediction length/distance analysis (Figure 7 and appendix figures) shows substantial fluctuation and non-monotonic patterns, and the paper acknowledges the decoding trends only 'somewhat' match the verification experiment; the narrative of consistent temporal-scale effects is stronger than the data visibly support.
No code or released artifacts are mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the model's complexity (200M parameters, custom fMRI preprocessing pipelines for two dataset formats).

Some presentation issues: the verification findings in Section 2 are reported via a forward reference to Figure 12 in the appendix before the main results are shown; ROI definitions differ between LeBel (only 'Auditory' region) and Narratives (six Destrieux regions), making the cross-dataset BPC comparison somewhat inconsistent; a few equations/notation (e.g., FIR transformation dimensions) require careful parsing.

The claim of being 'first to investigate the impact of predictive coding phenomenon on fMRI-to-text decoding' is plausible but stated without qualification, and related work on predictive/surprisal-based decoding could be more thoroughly distinguished.
